Our story

This account is accurate to our actual timeline, including real dates. We’ve left out the city, the clinic, and other people’s names — everything else here happened as described.

How it started

On March 24, 2026, our vet in Canada confirmed the ISO-compliant microchip our dog has had since 2014, gave his second rabies vaccination (the first was in 2024), and drew blood for the antibody test Japan requires — all in one visit. Japan allows the blood draw on the same day as the second vaccination; a dog starting from scratch couldn’t compress it this far, because the chip has to come first, then two vaccinations at least 30 days apart, and only then the blood draw. That single date became the anchor for everything downstream: a 180-day minimum wait before travel, a 2-year outer limit on the test result, and a chain of booster and retest deadlines that all trace back to it.

Four separate pieces had to line up correctly: the right kind of microchip, the right kind of rabies vaccine, a blood sample sent to a lab Japan actually recognizes, and a Japan-specific import form that our own country’s standard export paperwork doesn’t cover. A fifth complication sat underneath all of it — our dog has a heart condition, and a possible surgery meant the travel date itself couldn’t be treated as fixed.

Advice that needed a second look

A vet mentioned, in passing, that our documents needed blue-ink signatures. We couldn’t find that requirement in Japan’s rules, and an original document isn’t something you casually redo, so we chased it down. Japan’s official import guide specifies no signature ink color at all — it rules out pencil, erasable ink and correction fluid, which is a different requirement — and a designated lab’s own FAQ says a black-ink signature on the antibody test report is fine. We were ready to call it a myth. Then CFIA told us in writing that it does require a wet blue-ink signature from our vet on the rabies vaccination certificates we bring to the endorsement appointment, and recommended a wet-ink signature on the original Japan health certificate. The vet was right — just about a different document, and a different authority, than we first assumed. The lesson: Japan’s rules and your own export authority’s rules are separate, so check each one directly.

The same pattern showed up with the export certificate itself. Our home country issues a standard, generic international health certificate that covers exporting an animal to most destinations. Japan is not “most destinations”: it has its own recommended form, any certificate it accepts has to cover everything on that form, and our own country’s official guidance says not to use the generic certificate when the destination country supplies its own. We only caught this by reading past the first search result and cross-checking two official sources against each other — and it changed which document our vet actually needed to complete.

The country nobody could agree on

The most genuinely unresolved question we ran into wasn’t about Japan at all — it was about our own route there. Our dog lives in Canada, was microchipped and vaccinated in Canada, and had blood drawn in Canada that was then shipped to a laboratory in the United States, simply because that’s where an approved lab exists. Our travel plan adds a third leg: driving from Canada into the United States, an overnight stay, then a direct flight to Japan from a U.S. airport the next day — under 24 hours on U.S. soil in total.

That raises a specific question: for Japan’s paperwork, which country is the exporting country — Canada, where our dog lives and where every vaccination and test actually took place, or the United States, where the international flight physically departs from? We asked this in more than one place and got two different confident answers. A Canada-focused resource treated Canada as the exporting country by default and didn’t address the U.S. leg at all. A resource focused on airline and airport requirements framed the country of departure as what matters, which points to the United States instead. Neither source was wrong on its own terms — each was answering from its own slice of the process, and neither accounted for a route that touches both countries.

We have not found one authoritative source that resolves this directly. The practical consequence: we are arranging export certification from both countries — a Canadian-endorsed certificate through our own official channel, and a U.S.-endorsed one as well — rather than guessing which one gets checked at the airport. That’s more paperwork and more cost than either certificate alone. Given how much a wrong guess would cost us, redundancy is the correct trade.

Deadlines that fail in two different ways

Once the vaccination and blood test were done, the real planning started, because that test result has a shelf life, and it can expire in two different ways with two very different consequences. The result must be at least 180 days old before travel, and it stays valid for 2 years total from the draw date — but only if our dog’s rabies vaccine coverage never lapses in between. From our March 24, 2026 draw date, that gave us a window opening in late September 2026 and closing in March 2028.

Those two limits fail differently. If our travel date ever slipped past the 2-year mark, that’s recoverable: we’d get a second blood test. We first assumed that would start a new 180-day clock, but Japan’s own import guide says otherwise — as long as rabies coverage never lapsed and the second draw is at least 180 days after the first (ours easily would be), the new result counts as soon as it’s back from the lab, with no second wait. If a rabies booster were ever given even a day after the previous one’s labeled protection period ended, the entire process resets — new vaccination series, new blood test, new 180-day wait, six-plus months undone by one missed appointment. Because the two failures cost so differently, we treat them differently: a retest only needs enough lead time for the lab result to come back, while every future booster gets closer to six weeks of margin — marked on an actual calendar, not left to memory.

Why this was never just paperwork

Our dog’s heart condition meant a real chance of surgery interrupting our timeline. Understanding exactly how much flexibility the 180-day and 2-year rules actually allow — and confirming that a delayed trip costs us nothing as long as vaccine coverage stays unbroken — separated a medical decision from a paperwork deadline. That distinction mattered more to us than any individual form.

Why we’re sharing this

None of this was insurmountable. It took more research and more cross-checking than it should have, because well-meaning advice was sometimes accurate, sometimes outdated, and sometimes simply built for a route that crosses one country instead of three. We built this tool so the next person starts with a clearer map — including an honest account of the one question we still haven’t fully resolved. If you find a more definitive answer on the exporting-country question than we have, tell us: it’s the single biggest gap left in this checklist.

This is a community tool, not legal or veterinary advice. Rules for importing animals into Japan can change, and every situation has its own details. Always confirm current requirements with your veterinarian, your country's export authority, and Japan's Animal Quarantine Service (AQS) before you travel.
